title: Honest uncertainty builds trust
text: Users report higher trust when the navigation companion admits uncertainty or owns its mistakes, while repeated errors or lack of honest cues reduce trust.
evidence: T2: Honestly I only trust the companion when it admits it is unsure. It once said it could not find the lab and asked me to look for a sign, and that made me trust it more.
N1: A good companion speaks rarely, shows the next step only, and owns its mistakes. Trust is built less by accuracy than by honest uncertainty.
T3: But when it gave me the wrong turn twice I stopped believing it. I wish I could switch off the chatter in quiet places like the reading room.

title: Cognitive load from visual and auditory clutter
text: Frequent visual overlays and excessive voice instructions distract users, causing them to look away, stop listening, or dismiss the companion.
evidence: N1: Navigation aids in mixed reality fail when they compete for attention. Designers keep adding overlays, but pedestrians need a calm view of the real street.
T1: The first time [participant] showed me the companion, it talked too much and I stopped listening.
T2: Too many pop-ups pull my attention away from the corridor and I nearly walked into a glass door.
N2: One participant stopped mid-corridor to dismiss a notification.

title: Social visibility and physical discomfort
text: Wearing a heavy mixed‑reality headset in public makes users feel self‑conscious because people stare, and it can cause physical discomfort such as dizziness.
evidence: T3: [participant] from my hostel said the glasses made him dizzy. People stare when I speak to it, so I mostly use the arrows.
N1: Wearing a heavy headset in public also carries a social cost, because people react to what they cannot see.
T2: I would feel silly talking to a companion in front of other people. At home it feels fine, in a crowded lobby it does not.

title: Modality preference and readability
text: Participants prefer glanceable arrow cues over voice instructions, and they experience visual fatigue from small text and physical fatigue from wearing the headset for extended periods.
evidence: T1: I wear the headset when I walk through a new campus building because the arrows on the floor save me from stopping every minute.
N2: In the pilot, two of three participants returned to arrows after the voice mode misheard place names. Observers saw frequent glances at the floor and at phones.
T2: [participant] told me that voice instructions work better for her, but I prefer arrows because I can glance at them. The device is heavy after twenty minutes.
T1: After a long walk my eyes get tired and the small text is hard to read.

title: Companion as social anchor
text: The navigation companion reduces feelings of isolation by greeting users by name and offering a sense of companionship during exploration.
evidence: T3: As a new student I felt isolated in the first week and the companion gave me a reason to explore. It remembered where the library was and greeted me by name, which felt friendly.
T1: Sometimes I forget I am alone in the corridor, and that feels good. My friend [participant] asked me to write to [email] or call [phone] if I want to try it again.
